**Xu Zhiyong** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 许志永; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Xǔ Zhìyǒng*; born March 2, 1973) is a Chinese civil rights activist and formerly a lecturer at the [Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_University_of_Post_and_Telecommunications "Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications"). He was one of the founders of the NGO [Open Constitution Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Constitution_Initiative "Open Constitution Initiative") and an active rights lawyer in China who campaigned against corruption[[1]](#cite_note-1) and helped those underprivileged. He is the main founder and icon of the [New Citizens' Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Citizens'_Movement_(China) "New Citizens' Movement (China)") in China. In January 2014 he was sentenced to four years in prison for "gathering crowds to disrupt public order".[[2]](#cite_note-bbc1-2) He was detained again on February 15, 2020, in the southern city of [Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou "Guangzhou") after two months in hiding, for his participation in a meeting of rights activists and lawyers in [Xiamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiamen "Xiamen") in December 2019 in which "democratic transition in China" was discussed.[[3]](#cite_note-3) He was sentenced for subversion to 14 years in jail on April 10, 2023.[[4]](#cite_note-nyt_20230410-4)

Xu was born in [Minquan County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minquan_County "Minquan County"), [Henan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henan "Henan") Province in 1973. He was married to Cui Zheng (崔筝), a journalist. Their daughter was born on January 13, 2014, while Xu was in a detention center facing trial.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) He had been in hiding since late 2019 and was detained by Chinese police on February 15, 2020.[[7]](#cite_note-7) In March 2021, his partner [Li Qiaochu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Qiaochu "Li Qiaochu") was reported to have been arrested for tweeting that Xu and another activist had been tortured while in detention.[[8]](#cite_note-scmp_20210315-8)

## Career and activism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Xu_Zhiyong&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career and activism")]

Xu received his Bachelor of Law degree from [Lanzhou University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanzhou_University "Lanzhou University") in 1994 and Doctor of Law degree from [Peking University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_University "Peking University") in 2002.

In 2003, he was elected to the [Haidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haidian_District "Haidian District") District People's Congress as an [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_(politics) "Independent (politics)"). He won the re-election in 2006.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In the 2011 election, Xu was excluded from the official candidate list due to government pressure and he lost to [Fang Binxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fang_Binxing "Fang Binxing") ("*Father of China's Great Firewall*"), but he still gathered more than 3,500 votes out of 22,000 voters in his district as a [write-in candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Write-in_candidate "Write-in candidate").

Xu helped found the public interest group Gongmeng, also known as the [Open Constitution Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Constitution_Initiative "Open Constitution Initiative").[[10]](#cite_note-hric_20090319-10)

Unlike other human rights activists, Xu firmly and carefully pushed his calls for political change and social justice in existing laws, and his group has been regarded as relatively cautious and conservative.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12) In his recent interview before his arrest, he described his dream as follows:

> I wish our country could be a free and happy one. Every citizen need not go against their conscience and can find their own place by their virtue and talents; a simple and happy society, where the goodness of humanity is expanded to the maximum, and the evilness of humanity is constrained to the minimum; honesty, trust, kindness, and helping each other are everyday occurrences in life; there is not so much anger and anxiety, a pure smile on everyone's face.

— Xu Zhiyong[[13]](#cite_note-13)

Xu's final remarks post trial also made rounds within Chinese dissident communities abroad in which he described goal of the New Citizens' Movement as follows:

> What the New Citizens Movement advocates is for each and every Chinese national to act and behave as a citizen, to accept our roles as citizens and masters of our country—and not to act as feudal subjects, remain complacent, accept mob rule or a position as an underclass. To take seriously the rights which come with citizenship, those written into the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and China's Constitution: to treat these sacred rights—to vote, to freedom of speech and religion—as more than an everlasting IOU.

— Xu Zhiyong (2014)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

### The 2009 Gongmeng incident

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Xu_Zhiyong&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The 2009 Gongmeng incident")]

On July 29, 2009, he was arrested at his home, and detained by Chinese authorities on charges of tax evasion.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[10]](#cite_note-hric_20090319-10) At the same time Xu's colleague [Zhuang Lu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhuang_Lu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zhuang Lu (page does not exist)") was also arrested by authorities.[[17]](#cite_note-release-17)

The Open Constitution Initiative was fined 1.46 million [RMB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renminbi "Renminbi") on July 14, 2009, for 'dodging taxes' and was shut down by the authorities by declaring it "illegal".[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Xu Zhiyong was released on bail on August 23, 2009.[[17]](#cite_note-release-17)[[19]](#cite_note-19) The Australian newspaper *[The Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Age "The Age")* reported that the release of Xu, Zhuang and another Chinese dissident, [Ilham Tohti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilham_Tohti "Ilham Tohti"), was in part due to pressure on Beijing from the administration of American President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").[[20]](#cite_note-age-20)

### Post-Gongmeng era, New Citizens' Movement, 2013 arrest

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Xu_Zhiyong&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Post-Gongmeng era, New Citizens' Movement, 2013 arrest")]

After Gongmeng was shut down, Xu Zhiyong and supporters adopted the name "Citizens" to continue their cause. In May 2012, Xu formally established the "New Citizens' Movement" and "New Citizens' Spirit" as the high-level concept of their activism.

In 2013, Xu was placed under house arrest for more than three months, before being formally arrested on August 22.[[21]](#cite_note-21) His trial started on January 22, 2014. Xu and his lawyer Zhang Qingfang remained silent throughout the trial (except for his closing statement) to protest the violation of basic legal procedure. Xu's closing statement was cut short by the judge, but the text was circulated on the internet[[22]](#cite_note-22) and raised tremendous support.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] On January 26, Xu was sentenced to four years in prison for "gathering crowds to disrupt public order".[[2]](#cite_note-bbc1-2) Prior to the verdict, whose date had been expected, lawyer Zhang said about the case: "We can say it was decided even before the trial."[[23]](#cite_note-23) He was released in 2017.[[24]](#cite_note-cnn_20230410-24)

Xu and other human rights activists were wanted by police for their participation in a meeting in [Xiamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiamen "Xiamen") on December 13, 2019[[25]](#cite_note-nyt_20200217-25)[[26]](#cite_note-rfa_20210208-26) where "democratic transition in China" was discussed.[[8]](#cite_note-scmp_20210315-8) In February 2020, while in hiding, through postings on social media, Xu publicly asked [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_China "Communist Party of China") [general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Communist_Party_of_China "General Secretary of the Communist Party of China") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") to resign, for what he described

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about a person whose name includes a [patronymic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"). The article properly refers to the person by her given name, Rahile, and not as Dawut.

| Rahile Dawut | |
| --- | --- |
| [Raile Dawut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rahile_Dawut.jpg) Raile Dawut in 2006 | |
| Born | 20 May 1966 (age 60)  [Ürümqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi "Ürümqi"), Xinjiang, China |
| Occupation | Anthropologist |
| Criminal charge | Endangering state security |
| Criminal penalty | [Life imprisonment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_imprisonment "Life imprisonment") |

**Rahile Dawut** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 热依拉·达吾提; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Rèyīlā Dáwútí*; [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghur_language "Uyghur language"): راھىلە داۋۇت; born 20 May 1966) is a Uyghur ethnographer known for her expertise in [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") [folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore "Folklore") and [traditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghur_culture "Uyghur culture"). Formerly a professor at [Xinjiang University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_University "Xinjiang University"), where she founded the Minorities Folklore Research Centre, she was [disappeared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearance "Enforced disappearance") by the [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") in 2017 and has not been seen since.

Rahile was sentenced to life imprisonment on separatist charges in 2020.

## Early life and career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rahile_Dawut&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Rahile was born to an [intellectual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual "Intellectual") family in [Ürümqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi "Ürümqi"). In 1998, she earned her PhD at [Beijing Normal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Normal_University "Beijing Normal University"), as the first Uyghur woman to do so.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Rahile was previously a member of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") for over 30 years. After marrying, she gave birth to her daughter Akida Pulat. She pursued advanced studies in Beijing, with her parents assisting in childcare. Prior to her detention, she taught at Xinjiang University, where she founded the Minorities Folklore Research Center in 2007 and served as its director.[[3]](#cite_note-thediplomat_20201123-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) Rahile has published a number of articles and books, and has also delivered lectures at universities internationally, including [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") and the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge").[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-bbc1-6) Her 2002 study on religious shrines became popular among Uyghur farmers, who used it as a guide for pilgrimages. In December 2018, she was secretly tried and convicted of "splittism", resulting in a life sentence. Her appeal was subsequently rejected.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
Her research has been credited with preserving Uyghur cultural heritage at a time of increasing state suppression. Through her documentation of sacred sites and oral histories, Dawut helped record traditions that were otherwise at risk of disappearing under state-driven assimilation policies.[[8]](#cite_note-SmithFinley2019-8)[[9]](#cite_note-Byler2018-9) Scholars noted that her work not only contributed to the field of ethnography but also served as a form of cultural resistance by affirming Uyghur identity through academic rigor.[[10]](#cite_note-Roberts2020-10)

## Disappearance, trial and jailing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Rahile_Dawut&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Disappearance, trial and jailing")]

In December 2017, Rahile reportedly told a relative of her plans to travel from [Ürümqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi "Ürümqi") to [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), after which her family and friends lost contact with her. Rahile's family and friends announced her disappearance in August 2018.[[11]](#cite_note-Rahile_Dawut,_China-11) By the end of 2018, it was known that she was in the hands of Chinese state authorities.[[12]](#cite_note-12) According to an article in *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, Rahile was one of a number of prominent intellectuals targeted as part of China's [campaign to erase Uyghur identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Uyghurs_in_China "Persecution of Uyghurs in China").[[13]](#cite_note-13) State authorities have not publicly disclosed Rahile's whereabouts.

Rahile's secret trial began in December 2018 in a Xinjiang court, where she was first found guilty of "endangering state security".[[14]](#cite_note-:0-14) She was reportedly jailed for life as she lost her appeal against the charges in September 2023.[[14]](#cite_note-:0-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16) The [Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People's Republic of China") spokesperson [Mao Ning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Ning_(diplomat) "Mao Ning (diplomat)") said she had "no information" on the case.[[6]](#cite_note-bbc1-6)

Rahile's disappearance and sentencing have drawn significant international condemnation. In 2018, the Central Eurasian Studies Society expressed strong concern over her detention, highlighting her contributions to the preservation of Uyghur culture. In 2020, the Open Society University Network named her an Honorary Professor in the Humanities, acknowledging her scholarly impact. Rahile's daughter, Akida Pulat, has been actively campaigning for her mother's release, bringing attention to her case on international platforms. Human rights organizations, including PEN America, have cited Rahile's disappearance as part of broader attempts to erase Uyghur culture.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) The United States condemned China's reported life sentence of Rahile, calling for her immediate release.[[19]](#cite_note-19)
Scholars and researchers argue that Dawut's disappearance fits into a broader pattern of targeting Uyghur intellectuals and dismantling Uyghur cultural infrastructure. According to Sean R. Roberts and Joanne Smith Finley, the repression of cultural figures like Dawut is part of a campaign to erase the distinct ethnic and religious identity of the Uyghur people through state policy.[[8]](#cite_note-SmithFinley2019-8)[[10]](#cite_note-Roberts2020-10)

Academic institutions and advocacy groups highlighted her case in calls for greater protection of scholars at risk. In public statements and reports, organizations such as Scholars at Risk and PEN International have emphasized that Dawut's detention undermines academic freedom and violates international human rights standards.[[20]](#cite_note-PENAmerica2023-20)[[21]](#cite_note-HRW2023-21)

In October 2025, United Nation's Special Rapporteurs, and Independent Experts and Working Groups expressed serious concern over the enforced disappearance of Rahile. The experts stated that Rahile's case "reflect deeply troubling patterns where cultural identity, artistic creativity, and academic work are treated as threats to national security", and "The right to freely express and participate in cultural life, without discrimination or fear, is a cornerstone of human rights."[[22]](#cite_note-ohchr_2025-22)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Ding Jiaxi | |
| --- | --- |
| 丁家喜 | |

**Ding Jiaxi** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 丁家喜; born 17 August 1967) is a Chinese civil rights activist known for co-organizing the [New Citizens' Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Citizens'_Movement "New Citizens' Movement") advocating for political change in China. Ding was detained, along with other human rights activists, in 2019 after having a dinner together in [Xiamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiamen "Xiamen") with other human rights activists to discuss social issues.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-rfa2021-3) He was then sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2022 for subversion of state power. According to Ding's wife, evidence for charges against Ding and other detainees include "participating in a [Telegram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_(software) "Telegram (software)") group chat, articles and online posts, and organizing classes in non-violent resistance."[[3]](#cite_note-rfa2021-3)

Ding was the recipient of the U.S. [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_State "Department of State")'s Global Human Rights Defender Award in 2023.[[4]](#cite_note-dos2023-4) In 2024, Ding was nominated for the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") due to his "commitment to human rights and peace in China" by the chairs of [Congressional-Executive Commission on China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional-Executive_Commission_on_China "Congressional-Executive Commission on China").[[5]](#cite_note-cecc_letter-5)

In June 2022, Ding and [Xu Zhiyong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Zhiyong "Xu Zhiyong") were given prison sentences for 14 and 12 years, respectively, after a closed-door trial in June 2022. The convictions were described as farcical by [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In 2024, [Freedom House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House "Freedom House") reported that Ding's communication with family members have been restricted to letters. Prison authorities told Ding's wife to "forget about it, Ding will never be allowed a phone call with you."[[7]](#cite_note-Freedom_House_2024-7)

## International response

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ding_Jiaxi&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: International response")]

Before Ding's conviction, on 18 March 2022 ahead of the EU–China summit, NGOs including [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch"), [World Uyghur Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Uyghur_Congress "World Uyghur Congress"), and [Front Line Defenders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_Line_Defenders "Front Line Defenders") sent a joint letter to the Presidents of the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") and [European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council "European Council"), urging the EU and its member states to, among other things, publicly call for the release of detained human rights defenders in China, including Ding.[[8]](#cite_note-HRW_March_2022-8)

The [United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_High_Commissioner_for_Human_Rights "United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights") [Volker Türk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volker_T%C3%BCrk "Volker Türk") stated in April 2023 that "I am very concerned that two prominent human rights defenders in China – Ding Jiaxi and Xu Zhiyong – have been sentenced to lengthy prison terms, at variance with international human rights law standards."[[9]](#cite_note-ohchr-9)

Ding, along with Xu and human rights lawyer [Chow Hang-tung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chow_Hang-tung "Chow Hang-tung"), received the [Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Bars_and_Law_Societies_of_Europe "Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe") (CCBE) Human Rights Award 2023 for their "courage, determination and commitment to defending human rights and the rule of law in China". CCBE President Panagiotis Perakis stated that "European lawyers will continue to closely monitor the situation and support their Chinese colleagues who need help. We will never accept that lawyers are targeted because of their legitimate activities as lawyers."[[10]](#cite_note-ccbe-10)

Ding was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 2024 by chairs of the [Congressional-Executive Commission on China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional-Executive_Commission_on_China "Congressional-Executive Commission on China") [Christopher Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Smith_(New_Jersey_politician) "Chris Smith (New Jersey politician)") and [Jeff Merkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Merkley "Jeff Merkley"), commending on Ding's "deep commitment to human rights and peace in China".[[5]](#cite_note-cecc_letter-5)

**Guo Feixiong** ([simplified Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 郭飞雄; [traditional Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 郭飛雄; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Guō Fēixióng*) born 2 August 1966)[[1]](#cite_note-1) is the pen name of **Yang Maodong** (杨茂东/楊茂東), a Chinese human rights legal activist from [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong "Guangdong") province who is often identified with the [Weiquan movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weiquan_movement "Weiquan movement"). Guo is known as a dissident writer and "[barefoot lawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barefoot_lawyer "Barefoot lawyer")", who has worked on several controversial issues to defend the [rights of marginalized groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_rights "Minority rights"). Prior to his 2006 imprisonment, Guo worked as a legal advisor to the Shanghai Shengzhi Law Firm.[[2]](#cite_note-HRIC-2)

Guo was born on 1966 in [Gucheng County, Hebei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gucheng_County,_Hebei "Gucheng County, Hebei"). During the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), he was sent to the countryside with his parents for nine years, where they experienced poverty. In July 1988, he graduated from the Department of Philosophy of [East China Normal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_China_Normal_University "East China Normal University") in Shanghai, and was assigned to work at [Wuhan Medical College for Staff and Workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jianghan_University "Jianghan University"), where he served as a philosophy teacher. Guo actively participated in the [1989 Tiananmen Square Protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_Protests "1989 Tiananmen Square Protests"). In 1991 he went to [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong "Guangdong"), where he was engaged in various occupations. From 1993 to 2001, he mainly engaged in private publishing, and then made a living by writing.[[3]](#cite_note-WEI-3)

In 2005 and 2006, human rights groups reported that Guo was taken into custody and beaten on multiple occasions for his [human rights advocacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_defender "Human rights defender"), including his work on the [Taishi village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taishi,_Guangzhou "Taishi, Guangzhou") standoff. The beating of Guo Feixiong was reportedly one of the catalysts behind a rolling nationwide hunger strike organized by Guo's friend and associate [Gao Zhisheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gao_Zhisheng "Gao Zhisheng").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Guo was arrested on 30 September 2006 and detained on charges of "illegal business activity" connection with the publication of a book on a political scandal in [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning "Liaoning") province, *Shenyang Political Earthquake*. After being held in pre-trial detention for 17 months, he was sentenced to five years of imprisonment at the Meizhou Prison on 14 November 2007 in what was characterized as a "trial marked with serious procedural irregularities."[[5]](#cite_note-5) In addition to his sentence, Guo was fined 40,000 yuan. Family members reported that Guo was [tortured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture") in custody, deprived of sleep, and shocked with [electric batons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroshock_weapon#Torture "Electroshock weapon").[[2]](#cite_note-HRIC-2)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Guo was released on 13 September 2011, and stated that he remained committed to the cause of human rights advocacy.[[2]](#cite_note-HRIC-2)

On 8 August 2013, Guo was again arrested on suspicion of "gathering a crowd to disrupt order in a public place". On 10 December 2013, the Tianhe District Branch of the Guangzhou Municipal Public Security Bureau recommended that Guo be indicted for the crime of "gathering a crowd to disrupt order in a public place", along with Sun Desheng, another activist.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

On 29 October 2013, the [United States House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Africa, Global Health, Global Human Rights and International Organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Foreign_Affairs_Subcommittee_on_Africa,_Global_Health,_Global_Human_Rights_and_International_Organizations "United States House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Africa, Global Health, Global Human Rights and International Organizations") held a hearing on the circumstances surrounding China's detention of Guo Feixiong.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Guo is the recipient of the 2015 [Front Line Defenders Award for Human Rights Defenders at Risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_Line_Defenders#Front_Line_Defenders_Award_for_Human_Rights_Defenders_at_Risk "Front Line Defenders").[[9]](#cite_note-Thoolen_2015-9)

On 28 January 2021, Guo was arrested by the border inspection on the grounds of 'endangering national security' at [Shanghai Pudong International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Pudong_International_Airport "Shanghai Pudong International Airport"), when he was about to board a flight to the United States to visit his cancer-stricken wife.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Guo was again detained in December 2021 and formally arrested on the charge of "subversion to state power" on 12 January 2022, two days after the death of his wife, Zhang Qing, in the United States. He had repeatedly pleaded with authorities to be allowed to visit her and his children after she had been diagnosed in January 2021 with terminal illness.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Following the death of Zhang in January 2022, [U.S. Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State") spokesperson [Ned Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Price "Ned Price") issued a statement where he requested that the Chinese authorities must grant Guo humanitarian relief and allow his travel to the United States to be reunited with his children and grieve the passing of his wife.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

On 11 May 2023, Guo was found guilty of inciting subversion of state power to a prison term of eight years. Diplomats from several countries, including the U.S. embassy, said they were prevented from attending the trial. The U.S. embassy in China said that they “continue to call for Mr. Guo's speedy release so he may be reunited with his family."[[13]](#cite_note-13)

Guo was married to Zhang Qing, with whom he had two children; a son and a daughter. Zhang and children fled their [Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou "Guangzhou") home in January 2009 and fled to the United States from Thailand, where they were granted political asylum in November that year.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) From the US, Zhang continued to advocate for the freedom of her husband.[[16]](#cite_note-16) In January 2021, Zhang was diagnosed with late-stage [colon cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colon_cancer "Colon cancer"). As a result, Guo sent an open letter where he requested to be allowed to leave China and reunite with her,[[17]](#cite_note-17) which was rejected by the authorities. He was arrested in January 2021 at Shanghai airport as he tried to visit his dying wife. [[18]](#cite_note-18) Zhang died on 10 January 2022, at the age of 55.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

Drinks and canned yellow peaches were laid at the school gate, with flowers of condolence visible afar.

The roof of the school [gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gym "Gym") of the No 34 Middle School of [Qiqihar, Heilongjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiqihar "Qiqihar"), China collapsed on 23 July 2023 at 14:56 local time, killing 11 people with another four injured.[[1]](#cite_note-reuters-01-1)[[2]](#cite_note-ap-01-2)

The No 34 Middle School of Qiqihar is a public [secondary school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_school "Secondary school") located in the city’s [Longsha District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longsha_District "Longsha District") and offers [lower secondary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_secondary_education "Lower secondary education") (Level 2).[[3]](#cite_note-qqhd-01-3) Qiqihar is a [prefecture-level city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefecture-level_city "Prefecture-level city") with a population of about 5 million, the second-largest in the northernmost and easternmost province of China, [Heilongjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang "Heilongjiang").[[4]](#cite_note-scmp-01-4) The school’s gym that collapsed in this incident is reported to be built in 1997[[5]](#cite_note-tg-01-5)[[6]](#cite_note-scmp-02-6) with an area of 1,200 square metres.[[7]](#cite_note-caixin-01-7)

The collapse happened on 23 July 2023 at 14:56 local time, according to the provincial fire and rescue department, reported by the [Xinhua News Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinhua_News_Agency "Xinhua News Agency").[[1]](#cite_note-reuters-01-1) The collapse resulted in the whole roof of the gym and the building materials made of perlite that were wrongly placed on it falling to the ground entirely. 19 people were inside the gym when the accident occurred; four managed to escape, with the rest 15 trapped; most were school children.[[1]](#cite_note-reuters-01-1)[[6]](#cite_note-scmp-02-6) The children are believed to be primarily students of a girls’ volleyball team of the very school or from nearby schools.[[8]](#cite_note-sohu-01-8) Reports claim they were training at the time of the collapse, and the team practising that day had reportedly just won second place in the provincial championship.[[9]](#cite_note-nyt-01-9)[[1]](#cite_note-reuters-01-1)[[5]](#cite_note-tg-01-5) Among the 15 trapped, two were coaches, and the rest 13 were children.[[10]](#cite_note-zaobao-01-10)[[11]](#cite_note-cnn-01-11)[[12]](#cite_note-scmp-03-12)

39 fire trucks and 159 rescuers were sent to the scene.[[4]](#cite_note-scmp-01-4) Eight were discovered by 17:30 local time,[[4]](#cite_note-scmp-01-4) with six more by dawn[[13]](#cite_note-times-01-13) and the last by around 10:00 the next day.[[14]](#cite_note-xh-01-14) Among the trapped, five were found dead upon discovery, six died despite receiving medical treatment, and the remaining four were rescued with injuries.[[15]](#cite_note-caixin-02-15) One trapped coach was among the rescued[[16]](#cite_note-bbc-01-16) and the other was confirmed to be dead.[[8]](#cite_note-sohu-01-8)[[9]](#cite_note-nyt-01-9)

## Causes of the accident and investigation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Qiqihar_school_gymnasium_collapse&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Causes of the accident and investigation")]

Upon preliminary investigation, the direct cause of the accident was believed to be improperly placed building materials on the gymnasium's roof. There was a construction project nearby, and the workers had stacked [perlite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perlite "Perlite") on the top of the gym for the sake of convenience. A 30 mm precipitation was reported that day, which might have led to the perlite absorbing a large amount of water and resulting in the roof's overloading and collapse.[[1]](#cite_note-reuters-01-1)[[6]](#cite_note-scmp-02-6)[[17]](#cite_note-bloomberg-01-17)[[5]](#cite_note-tg-01-5)[[13]](#cite_note-times-01-13) *[The Beijing News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beijing_News "The Beijing News")* carried an editorial to condemn the accident, criticising the lack of supervision on the construction site.[[1]](#cite_note-reuters-01-1) [Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan")’s official newspaper, the *Changjiang Daily*, on the other hand, urged the local authorities in Qiqihar to investigate whether the collapsed building was a ‘[tofu-dreg project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu-dreg_project "Tofu-dreg project")’ in the first place.[[6]](#cite_note-scmp-02-6)[[12]](#cite_note-scmp-03-12)

It is reported that the local police have detained those involved in the adjacent construction project for further investigation.[[9]](#cite_note-nyt-01-9)[[16]](#cite_note-bbc-01-16)[[13]](#cite_note-times-01-13) Managers of the involved construction firm are said to face criminal charges.[[18]](#cite_note-ap-02-18)

Sources of social media in mainland China claimed that a large number of police officers[[10]](#cite_note-zaobao-01-10)[[19]](#cite_note-bbc-02-19) were deployed to gather the parents of the victims and kept them under watch while sharing little to no information with them.[[9]](#cite_note-nyt-01-9) A video circulated on the internet has shown a devastated father claiming they were not updated with information for the first five to six hours, and they were not allowed to identify their children’s bodies. The claim was echoed by other parents in the video, as well as users of social platforms, criticising the lack of proper communication from the police officers, the local officials, the school, and the hospital.[[1]](#cite_note-reuters-01-1)[[17]](#cite_note-bloomberg-01-17)[[16]](#cite_note-bbc-01-16)[[5]](#cite_note-tg-01-5)[[13]](#cite_note-times-01-13) Online users also censured the official announcement for its over-highlighting how much effort has been made by the authorities while de-emphasising casualties.[[17]](#cite_note-bloomberg-01-17)

Flowers, canned yellow peaches[[i]](#cite_note-fn-01-21), candles, and drinks were laid at the front gate of the school starting the next day to convey people’s condolences; some were brought by the locals, while some were laid by couriers on behalf of remote mourners.[[9]](#cite_note-nyt-01-9)[[8]](#cite_note-sohu-01-8)[[11]](#cite_note-cnn-01-11)[[21]](#cite_note-caixin-03-22)

Officials of Qiqihar apologised to the public over the accident.[[12]](#cite_note-scmp-03-12)

[Human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") in the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) are severely curtailed. [Freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech_in_China "Freedom of speech in China"), [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press"), [freedom of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_China "Freedom of religion in China"), [freedom of assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_assembly "Freedom of assembly") and [workers' rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_rights "Labor rights") are restricted by the [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China"). The [Chinese political system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_China "Politics of China") is [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism"), with no freely elected national leaders, and repression of political opposition, as well as a lack of [an independent judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_independence "Judicial independence"), [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law"), and [due process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Due_process "Due process").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Human rights abuses by the Chinese government are prevalent, with extensive [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China"),[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) [mass surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance_in_China "Mass surveillance in China"),[[5]](#cite_note-5) and repression of [ethnic minorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_minorities_in_China "Ethnic minorities in China") and religious groups, including [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_China "Christianity in China"),[[a]](#cite_note-12) [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_China_(1912%E2%80%93present) "Islam in China (1912–present)"), [Tibetan Buddhists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_Buddhism "Tibetan Buddhism"), [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs"),[[12]](#cite_note-13)[[13]](#cite_note-14) and groups the government deems as "cults" such as [Falun Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falun_Gong "Falun Gong").

The [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") and government's stated view of human rights emphasizes [economic development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_development "Economic development"), material well-being, and national [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty").[[14]](#cite_note-McGregor-15) They have often challenged notions of individual [civil and political rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_and_political_rights "Civil and political rights") in [international human rights law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_human_rights_law "International human rights law") as being [universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_value "Universal value").[[15]](#cite_note-uc-16)[[16]](#cite_note-ds-17)

Academics, international [non-governmental organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization "Non-governmental organization") (NGOs) including [Human Rights in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_in_China_(organization) "Human Rights in China (organization)") and [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International"), human rights treaty bodies and the [United Nations Human Rights Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Council "United Nations Human Rights Council")'s [Universal Periodic Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Periodic_Review "Universal Periodic Review"),[[17]](#cite_note-18) as well as citizens, lawyers, and [dissidents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissident "Dissident") inside the country, have documented how the authorities in [mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") regularly sanction or organize abuses.[[18]](#cite_note-19)[[19]](#cite_note-20)[[20]](#cite_note-21) [Human rights groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_human_rights_organizations "China human rights organizations") have also raised concerns about the prevalent use of [capital punishment in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_China "Capital punishment in China"), the [one-child policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-child_policy "One-child policy") (prior to abolishing it in 2015), and human rights in [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"). In a human rights report that assesses social, economic, and political freedoms, China received the lowest ranking globally for safety from state actions and the right to assemble.[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-amnesty.org-23)

Some survey data has indicated that citizens of the PRC prioritize the right to survival over political rights and the [World Values Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Values_Survey "World Values Survey") finds that 72% are satisfied with the state of human rights in their country.

Some Chinese activist groups are trying to improve human rights. [Chinese human rights attorneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weiquan_movement "Weiquan movement") who take on cases related to these issues, however, often face harassment, disbarment, and arrest by the Chinese state.[[23]](#cite_note-HRW_Thin_Ice-24)[[24]](#cite_note-amnesty13-25)[[25]](#cite_note-26) [Democracy movements in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_movements_of_China "Democracy movements of China") have been repressed, most notably in the [1989 Tiananmen Square massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre "1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre").[[26]](#cite_note-27)

Since the [legal reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_history_of_China#1978-1981 "Legal history of China") of the late 1970s and 1980s, the CCP has officially moved to embrace the language of the [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law"), and it has also attempted to establish a modern [court system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_system_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Court system of the People's Republic of China"). During this process, it has enacted thousands of new laws and regulations, and it has begun to train more [legal professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_profession "Legal profession").[[23]](#cite_note-HRW_Thin_Ice-24) The concept of 'rule of law' has been emphasized in the [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_China "Constitution of China"), and the ruling party has embarked on campaigns to promote the idea that citizens have protection under the law. At the same time, however, a fundamental contradiction exists in the constitution itself, in which the CCP insists that its authority supersedes that of the law.[[27]](#cite_note-fordham-28) Thus, the constitution enshrines the rule of law and simultaneously stresses the principle that the "[leadership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generations_of_Chinese_leadership "Generations of Chinese leadership") of the Communist Party" holds primacy over the law and the legal system.[[28]](#cite_note-29)

The judiciary is not [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_independence "Judicial independence") of the CCP, and judges face political pressure; in many instances, private party committees dictate the outcome of cases.[[29]](#cite_note-30) In 2007, law and the judiciary were further subordinated to the interests of the CCP under the doctrine of the [Three Supremes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Supremes "Three Supremes").[[30]](#cite_note-31) In 2013, [Document Number Nine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Number_Nine "Document Number Nine") detailed the CCP's antipathy toward the rule of law. This has produced a system often described as "rule *by* law" (alluding to the CCP's power), rather than rule *of* law.[[31]](#cite_note-nytimes-32) Moreover, the legal system lacks protections for [civil rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_(Common_law) "Civil law (Common law)"), and often fails to uphold due process.[[32]](#cite_note-33) This is opposed to a system of [checks and balances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checks_and_balances "Checks and balances") or [separation of powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_powers "Separation of powers").[[33]](#cite_note-34) Scholars have noted that these characteristics of the legal system in China often undermine due process in practice, particularly in politically sensitive criminal cases handled by defense lawyers, as analyzed in *[Criminal Defense in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_Defense_in_China "Criminal Defense in China")*.[[34]](#cite_note-Cambridge_University_Press-35)

Foreign experts estimate that in 2000, there were between 1.5 million and 4 million people in prison in mainland China. The PRC does not allow outsiders to inspect its penal system.[[35]](#cite_note-Becker-36)

Rights in China resemble the European construct of [positive law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_law "Positive law"), informed by the legacy of the [Napoleonic Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Code "Napoleonic Code"), in which rights are created and granted by the state.[[36]](#cite_note-37): 60

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Wang Quanzhang | |
| --- | --- |
| Born | 15 February 1976 (age 50)  [Wulian County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wulian_County "Wulian County"), [Shandong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shandong "Shandong"), China |
| Occupation | Lawyer |

**Wang Quanzhang** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 王全璋; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Wáng Quánzhāng*, born 15 February 1976) is a Chinese [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_human_rights_law "International human rights law") [lawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawyer "Lawyer") from [Wulian County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wulian_County "Wulian County"), [Shandong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shandong "Shandong"). Wang is known for defending
clients in politically sensitive cases against the Chinese government, which led to his arrest in the [709 crackdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/709_crackdown "709 crackdown"). He was then sentenced to four and a half years in prison for subverting state power. After Wang's release in 2020, Wang has been monitored, his landlords have been pressured to evict his family, and his son has been barred from attending school.[[1]](#cite_note-AP_2023-1)[[2]](#cite_note-rfa_2023-2)

Wang is a lawyer of the Beijing Fengrui Law Firm. He graduated from the School of Law at [Shandong University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shandong_University "Shandong University") in 2000. In 2003, Wang passed the [National Judicial Exam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Judicial_Exam "National Judicial Exam"), and in 2007, formally began his lawyer career in [Jinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinan "Jinan"), Shandong.[[3]](#cite_note-3) He later moved to Beijing, where he specialized in human rights cases, defending victims subjected to [land expropriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_property_law#Rural_property_expropriation_procedure "Chinese property law"), [labour camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_labor_camps "Chinese labor camps") mistreatment, and prison abuse. He also defended [Falun Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Falun_Gong "Persecution of Falun Gong") practitioners who have been subjected to ongoing nationwide persecution.[[4]](#cite_note-latimes-2018-12-26-4)

Wang also worked for the [NGO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGO "NGO") China Action, now re-established as [Safeguard Defenders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safeguard_Defenders "Safeguard Defenders"), which was co-founded in 2009 by Swedish human rights activist [Peter Dahlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dahlin "Peter Dahlin") to train Chinese lawyers, journalists and small NGOs on Chinese law and to protect [human rights in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China"). Dahlin was arrested in China in January 2016, and subsequently deported.[[5]](#cite_note-bbc-2018-12-26-5)[[4]](#cite_note-latimes-2018-12-26-4)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## Harassment, arrest, and disappearance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wang_Quanzhang&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Harassment, arrest, and disappearance")]

On 3 April 2013, Wang defended a Falun Gong practitioner at the [Jingjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingjiang "Jingjiang") People's Court, pleading not guilty. Wang was subsequently placed under judicial custody for disrupting court order. The next day, over 100 lawyers co-signed a petition demanding video evidence and Wang's release, while about 50 people came outside of the court to show support for Wang, including over 20 lawyers. Wang was released on 6 April.[[7]](#cite_note-front_line_defenders-7)[[8]](#cite_note-BBC_Liu_Interview-8)

According to U.S.-based organization [Human Rights in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_in_China_(organization) "Human Rights in China (organization)"), when Wang handed over documents to the court, he was taking pictures to save a copy. Wang's phone was then confiscated, and Wang disappeared after the hearing finished.[[9]](#cite_note-BBC_Public_Letter_Report-9)

### Beating in June 2015

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wang_Quanzhang&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Beating in June 2015")]

On 18 June 2015, Wang defended some Falun Gong practitioners on trial in [Liaocheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaocheng "Liaocheng"), Shandong, but the presiding judge Wang Yingjun (王英军) constantly hindered his attempts to present legal arguments. Eventually the judge ordered him to be evicted from the court and he was then beaten by court officials.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

### Arrest and disappearance in August 2015

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Wang_Quanzhang&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Arrest and disappearance in August 2015")]

In August 2015 Wang was arrested as part of a nationwide crackdown on lawyers and human rights activists instigated by CCP general secretary Xi Jinping, known as the [709 crackdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/709_crackdown "709 crackdown"), as it started on July 9, 2015.[[11]](#cite_note-bbc-2017-05-22-11) After his arrest, the authorities gave a notice of arrest to his wife, Li Wenzu (李文足), but refused to provide any information on where he was being held or to allow any access to him by his family or by a lawyer. For more than three years no information on his whereabouts or even whether he was dead or alive was forthcoming. By summer 2017, all the lawyers and activists arrested during the July 2015 crackdown, except for Wang, had either been released or sentenced to prison. Only the fate of Wang remained unknown.[[5]](#cite_note-bbc-2018-12-26-5)

Many of those arrested during the 2015 crackdown made forced confessions of guilt in court or on television, so Wang's wife, Li Wenzu, suggested that the reason why her husband had not been put on trial was that he refused to make any confession of guilt: "I think it might be because my husband hasn't compromised at all; that's why his case remains unsolved."[[11]](#cite_note-bbc-2017-05-22-11)

In April 2018, in order to publicize the disappearance of her husband a thousand days earlier, Li Wenzu embarked on a twelve-day walk from Beijing to [Tianjin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tianjin "Tianjin"), where she thought Wang may have been held. Li was accompanied on her march to Tianjin by Wang Qiaoling, the wife of lawyer [Li Heping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Heping "Li Heping"), who had also been arrested as part of the crackdown, and had been given a suspended sentence in April 2017.[[12]](#cite_note-bbc-2018-04-04-12) Li Wenzu was stopped from completing the march by the authorities.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

In July 2018, almost three years after his disappearance, Wang was finally allowed access to a lawyer, Liu Weiguo. According to Liu, Wang had not suffered any "hard violence" during his detention, which Li Wenzu interpreted to mean that he was subjected to other forms of mistreatment such as sleep deprivation and forced medication: "When Quanzhang said that he did not suffer hard violence, he was trying to tell me that he suffered inhuman torment!"[[14]](#cite_note-14)

In mid-December 2018, Li Wenzu and three other women publicly shaved their heads in the streets of Beijing as a protest against the continuing detention of Wang Quanzhang without trial.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Wang was finally put on trial for [subverting state power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inciting_subversion_of_state_power "Inciting subversion of state power") at the No. 2 Intermediate People's Court in Tianjin on 26 December 2018, some three and a half years after his initial disappearance. Court documents accuse Wang of working with the Swedish human rights activist [Peter Dahlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dahlin "Peter Dahlin") and others to "train hostile forces".[[5]](#cite_note-bbc-2018-12-26-5) Some activists and supporters were present outside the court, including [Yang Chunlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Chunlin "Yang Chunlin"), Zhang Zhecheng, and Xu Yan (wife of the detained lawyer Yu Wenshang), but they were forcibly removed or detained.[[4]](#cite_note-latimes-2018-12-26-4) Foreign journalists and diplomats were also denied entry to the courtroom.[[5]](#cite_note-bbc-2018-12-26-5) Wang's wife, Li Wenzu, was unable to attend the trial as she was prohibited from leaving her apartment in Beijing at 5 am on the day of the trial by security officials.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Within minutes of the trial starting on 26 December, Wang fired his court-appointed lawyer, causing the case to be immediately adjourned to an unspecified date so that another lawyer could be appointed for him. Commenting on this development, Dahlin said: "Wang is unlikely to get to choose his own lawyer, but this move will highlight the lack of any real trial being made available to him – that this is a show trial and nothing more".[[4]](#cite_note-latimes-2018-12-26-4) Protesters who had gathered outside the court in support of Wang were quickly removed by security police.[[17]](#cite_note-cnn_20190128-17)

On 28 December 2018, Li Wenzu and two other wives of detained lawyers (Yuan Shanshan 原珊珊, wife of Xie Yanyi 謝燕益, and Wang Xiaoling 王峭嶺, wife of [Li Heping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Heping "Li Heping")) tried to present a petition to the [Supreme People's Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Court "Supreme People's Court") at Hongsicun in [Chaoyang District, Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaoyang_District,_Beijing "Chaoyang District, Beijing"), protesting the handling of her husband's case by the Tianjin court. However, about fifty security officials surrounded her, and stopped her from entering the court building. She stated that she would try again the following week.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Large-scale [protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_and_dissent_in_China "Protest and dissent in China") and incidents of [civil disobedience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience "Civil disobedience") in the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") are described by [its government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") as "**mass incidents**" ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 群体性事件).[[1]](#cite_note-zonaeuropa-1)[[2]](#cite_note-china-org-cn-2)

The [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_government "Chinese government") broadly defines mass incidents as "planned or impromptu gathering[s] that form because of internal contradictions", and may include public speeches or demonstrations, physical clashes, public airings of grievances, and other group behaviors that are seen as disrupting social stability.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Through contemporary analysis of such events four key aspects of mass incidents have been identified "diversified participants, highly organized actions, easily escalated conflicts and thornier disputes to settle".[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4) Mass incidents have occurred in China because of the treatment of workers within [state-owned enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprises_of_China "State-owned enterprises of China") (SOEs) and [special economic zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China") (SEZs), the widening of [income disparities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_inequality_in_China "Income inequality in China"), and issues associated with development projects, namely forced land acquisition and environmental degradation.

Within the past few decades, the number of mass incidents occurring in China has seen significant growth, indicated by The Annual Report of China's Rules (2009).[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) In more recent times the numbers have continued to be high yet are less documented making reliable statistics rare, however it is definite that the frequency of mass incidents has increased.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Graph_of_Number_of_Mass_Incidents_in_China.jpg/250px-Graph_of_Number_of_Mass_Incidents_in_China.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graph_of_Number_of_Mass_Incidents_in_China.jpg)

Graph depicts the number of mass incidents that occurred in China from 1993 to 2006.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)

Mass incidents in China have been commonplace since the country's step towards socioeconomic transformation in the late 1970s, with incidents, described by Jiuchang Wei, as following this push for change like an "inseparable shadow".[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Mass incidents are characterized as any form of public disturbance. This includes any type of protesting, demonstrating, picketing as well as group petitioning.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) Those who are common participants in mass incidents include peasants, urban residents as well as workers within state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and special economic zones (SEZs).[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) Numbers of those involved can range from tens to thousands. The behaviors associated with mass incidents differ, some are peaceful, involving petitions, appeal to authorities for aid as well as collective walks and sit ins.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5)

Typically, there is a pattern to the collective behavior of mass incidents, with those occurring in rural areas to be of the more extreme nature than those in urban settings.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) This is because of less government involvement in country areas, meaning incidents have to reach severe levels for any intervention to occur.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) Despite this, city outbreaks of mass incidents are regarded as more serious, owing to the extreme effect they have on the government's image.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) Therefore, these areas are more controlled, in an attempt to prevent extreme behavior from occurring.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5)

The 2000s saw the height of social unrest within China, marked by the outbreak of numerous mass incidents.[[8]](#cite_note-8) This was because of immense economic, social and political issues which arose from much development within China. Each of these issues have caused misgoverning within policies surrounding the treatment of China's citizens, within areas of labor, development projects and legal systems.[[9]](#cite_note-:2-9)

### Layoffs and abuse of workers

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mass_incidents_in_China&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Layoffs and abuse of workers")]

[State-owned enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprises_of_China "State-owned enterprises of China") were the main source of urban employment in China during the early 1990s.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Therefore, the disbandment, restructuring and privatization of these institutions in 2000 led to millions of workers losing their source of income.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) Between 1999 and 2004 it was estimated that 27.8 million factory workers lost their jobs, resulting in masses of disgruntled workers and triggering urban mass incidents.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) These high rates of unemployment were met with the privatization of SOEs in which governments aimed to profit at the expense of their workers, leading to some of the largest mass incidents concerning labor occurring in March 2002.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) Including protests staged in front of city offices of 30,000 workers from 20 different factories in Liaoyang who complained of unpaid wages, corruption and the arrests of labor activists.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7)

The experiences of the SOE workers were mirrored within the [special economic zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China "Special economic zones of China") (SEZs). However, workers within SEZs possessed very limited understanding of labor rights because the workforce mainly consisted of uneducated female migrants from poor rural areas.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) This meant the workers were less likely to revolt despite suffering appalling conditions.[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) A set of data from 1992 of the [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong "Guangdong") province reported on the high death rate of workers and the presence of over 500,000 child laborers and 2003 data stated that a third of SEZ workers received less than minimum wage.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In 2004 these issues reached their height and with a combination of

# Lens 3B.1 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler protect residents from state violence, torture, disappearances, political imprisonment, extrajudicial killing, and arbitrary or exemplary punishment?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative** — Xi did not protect residents; the Chinese security apparatus continued mass internment in Xinjiang, escalated Hong Kong NSL prosecutions, broadened the legal-instrument framework (Counterespionage Law, Religious Activity Venues Measures, Patriotic Education Law), and handed down multiple long sentences to high-profile human-rights lawyers (Xu Zhiyong 14 years, Ding Jiaxi 12 years, Guo Feixiong 8 years, Yang Shaozheng 4.5 years, Qin Yongpei 5 years), with no independent national-level investigation or public correction of the security apparatus's conduct. The 2023 record also includes continued enforced disappearances, surveillance-tech tracking, and the use of the 2023 Uyghur-anthropologist life sentence (Rahile Dawut, September 2023) as exemplary punishment.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — political imprisonment continued and intensified in 2023

### 1. Xu Zhiyong sentenced to 14 years in prison on 10 April 2023

- **Claim A1.** On 10 April 2023, Xu Zhiyong, the founder of the Open Constitution Initiative and the New Citizens' Movement, was sentenced to 14 years in prison for "subversion of state power" by a closed-door trial. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk stated in April 2023 that the sentence was "at variance with international human rights law standards." Xu had been detained on 15 February 2020 after two months in hiding.
  - **Source:** "Xu Zhiyong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Zhiyong ("He was sentenced for subversion to 14 years in jail on April 10, 2023").
  - **Source:** "Comment by UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk on sentencing of human rights defenders in China" — *OHCHR*, April 10, 2023 — referenced in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ding_Jiaxi ("I am very concerned that two prominent human rights defenders in China – Ding Jiaxi and Xu Zhiyong – have been sentenced to lengthy prison terms, at variance with international human rights law standards").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.1 (strongly negative), 8D.7.

### 2. Ding Jiaxi sentenced to 12 years in prison; received US State Department Global Human Rights Defender Award 2023

- **Claim A2.** In 2022 (announced in 2023), Ding Jiaxi — co-organizer of the New Citizens' Movement — was sentenced to 12 years in prison for subversion of state power, after a closed-door trial. In 2023, Ding received the US Department of State Global Human Rights Defender Award. UN High Commissioner Türk criticized the sentence.
  - **Source:** "Ding Jiaxi" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ding_Jiaxi ("In June 2022, Ding and Xu Zhiyong were given prison sentences for 14 and 12 years, respectively, after a closed-door trial in June 2022. The convictions were described as farcical by Human Rights Watch").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.1 (strongly negative), 8D.7.

### 3. Guo Feixiong sentenced to 8 years in prison on 11 May 2023

- **Claim A3.** On 11 May 2023, Guo Feixiong, a long-time human-rights lawyer, was sentenced to 8 years in prison for "inciting subversion of state power." Diplomats from several countries, including the US embassy, said they were prevented from attending the trial. Guo's wife Zhang Qing had died of cancer in the US in January 2022; Guo had been denied permission to leave China to visit her before her death.
  - **Source:** "Guo Feixiong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guo_Feixiong ("On 11 May 2023, Guo was found guilty of inciting subversion of state power to a prison term of eight years. Diplomats from several countries, including the U.S. embassy, said they were prevented from attending the trial").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.1 (strongly negative), 8D.7.

### 4. Rahile Dawut life sentence upheld in September 2023; family not allowed to identify body

- **Claim A4.** Rahile Dawut, a Uyghur anthropologist, was disappeared in December 2017 and was sentenced to life imprisonment on "splittism" charges in a secret 2018 trial. Her appeal was rejected in **September 2023**, the Uyghur-focused mass-internment / forced-labor context intensifying through the 2023 calendar year. State authorities have not publicly disclosed her whereabouts.
  - **Source:** "Rahile Dawut" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahile_Dawut ("She was reportedly jailed for life as she lost her appeal against the charges in September 2023. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning said she had 'no information' on the case").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In September, a court sentenced prominent Uyghur anthropologist Dr. Rahile Dawut to life imprisonment").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.1 (strongly negative), 8D.5.

### 5. Yang Shaozheng sentenced to 4.5 years for "inciting subversion" in August 2023

- **Claim A5.** In August 2023, a court in Guizhou sentenced former economics professor Yang Shaozheng to 4.5 years in prison for "inciting subversion of state power" after he raised concerns about the high annual cost of government personnel in China.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In August, a court in Guizhou sentenced former economics professor, Yang Shaozheng, to 4.5 years in prison for 'inciting subversion of state power' after he raised concerns about the high annual cost of government personnel in China").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.1 (strongly negative), 8D.7.

## E. Net reading for lens 3B.1

The 2023 evidence is **strongly negative** on whether Xi protected residents from state violence, torture, disappearances, political imprisonment, extrajudicial killing, and arbitrary or exemplary punishment:

- **Mass imprisonment continued and intensified** in 2023, with multi-year sentences for human-rights lawyers (Xu Zhiyong 14 years, Ding Jiaxi 12 years, Guo Feixiong 8 years, Yang Shaozheng 4.5 years, Qin Yongpei 5 years, Kamile Wayit 3 years) and Uyghur intellectuals (Rahile Dawut life sentence upheld in September 2023).
- **Mass internment / forced-labor apparatus continued** in Xinjiang under Xi's August 2023 "success" declaration, with no independent inspection accepted.
- **Hong Kong NSL prosecutions continued** with the 47-trial proceeding through 2023 and Jimmy Lai's trial scheduled for December 2023.
- **Cross-border abductions** of journalist Yang Zewei (May 2023, Laos) and lawyer Lu Siwei (September 2023, deported from Laos) showed extraterritorial apparatus use.
- **Legal-instrument expansion** (Counterespionage Law, Religious Activity Venues Measures, Patriotic Education Law) increased state authority over civilians.
- **Surveillance-tech tracking** of LGBT users and journalists on TikTok/ByteDance.
- **Post-release harassment** of Wang Quanzhang and family continued through 2023.
- **Modest positives** (some White-Paper-protest detainees released; Fang Bin released) are outweighed by the dominant 2023 pattern.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have (a) released Xu Zhiyong, Ding Jiaxi, Guo Feixiong, Yang Shaozheng, Qin Yongpei, and the Hong Kong 47, (b) accepted independent inspection of Xinjiang, (c) repealed the Counterespionage Law expansion, (d) halted cross-border abductions, (e) lifted NSL prosecutions, (f) ordered independent national investigations into the 2023 mass-internment and forced-labor apparatus. Xi did the opposite on each.

**Net judgment: 3B.1 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi did not protect residents; the security apparatus continued mass internment, multiple long political sentences, NSL prosecutions, surveillance-tech tracking, and legal-instrument expansion. The 2023 record is one of expanded state authority over civilians and exemplary punishment of dissent.**
